history.heading: Indigenous peoples and Spanish rule
paragraphs: Before Spanish arrival, Costa Rica was a meeting point of Mesoamerican and South American cultures. The Diquís culture made hundreds of mysterious stone spheres, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the site of Guayabo was a large settlement.

Christopher Columbus landed on the Caribbean coast in 1502. The Spanish named it "rich coast", but there was little gold, and the colony remained poor and isolated, with small farms rather than large estates.

history.heading: Independence and coffee
paragraphs: Costa Rica became independent from Spain in 1821, was briefly part of Mexico and the Federal Republic of Central America, and became fully independent in 1838. Coffee exports from the 19th century brought prosperity and helped build roads, schools and the National Theatre.
In 1856 Costa Ricans defeated the American adventurer William Walker, who had seized control of Nicaragua.

history.heading: Abolition of the army
paragraphs: After a brief civil war in 1948, José Figueres Ferrer abolished the army, redirecting spending to education and health. Costa Rica has since been one of Latin America's most stable democracies. President Óscar Arias won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1987 for helping to end Central America's civil wars.

culture.heading: Pura vida
paragraphs: Costa Ricans, who call themselves Ticos, use the phrase "pura vida" as a greeting and philosophy of life. Spanish is the official language, and most people are Catholic, with a growing evangelical population. The Caribbean province of Limón has a large Afro-Caribbean community.

The national dish is gallo pinto (rice and beans), and the painted oxcart (carreta) is a national symbol recognised by UNESCO. Football is the most popular sport; the national team reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 2014.

politics.heading: Stable democracy
paragraphs: Costa Rica is a presidential republic with a single-chamber Legislative Assembly. Presidents serve four-year terms and cannot be re-elected consecutively. The country has no army, only police forces. Rising drug-related violence has become a major political concern.

economy.heading: From coffee to technology
paragraphs: Costa Rica has one of the higher living standards in Latin America. Exports have shifted from coffee and bananas to medical devices, electronics and services, attracted by free trade zones. Tourism, especially ecotourism, is a major industry: about a quarter of the country is protected, and it is famous for its biodiversity.
Almost all electricity comes from renewable sources. The currency is the colón. Costa Rica joined the OECD in 2021.
